extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTO officials, and appellate litigators (Federal Circuit)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and criteria for determining whether courts may review PTO Director decisions vacating ex parte reexamination proceedings (including application of 35 U.S.C. §§ 301–307, § 315(e)(1), and § 303(c)) under the Administrative Procedure Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'strong presumption' in favor of judicial review of administrative action (citing Cuozzo, Mach Mining, SAS Institute, Block).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That presumption may be overcome only by 'clear and convincing indications' that Congress intended to bar review, drawn from specific language, legislative history, and inferences from the statutory scheme as a whole. Where substantial doubt exists, the presumption controls. The court applies this presumption when assessing whether the ex parte reexamination statutory scheme precludes APA review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for statutory preclusion of review
rubrics_metrics.description: To find that a statute precludes judicial review, courts require clear and convincing evidence of congressional intent, based on specific statutory text, specific legislative history, and the statutory scheme in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a rigid evidentiary test but a reminder that general presumption for reviewability is controlling absent fairly discernible statutory intent to preclude. Cases like Block, Sackett, and Cuozzo frame the inquiry; courts look for detailed indicia of intent rather than merely plausible inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 35 U.S.C. § 303(c) (non-appealability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 303(c) states: 'A determination by the Director pursuant to subsection (a) of this section that no substantial new question of patentability has been raised will be final and nonappealable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision's preclusion is narrow and limited to denials under §303(a) that no substantial new question of patentability exists. It does not apply to determinations that a substantial new question exists, to §325(d) determinations, or to estoppel determinations under §315(e)(1). Courts must respect §303(c)'s textual limits and not expand its reach by implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text of 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(1) estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner in an inter partes review that results in a final written decision, or the real party in interest or privy, 'may not request or maintain a proceeding before the [PTO] with respect to that claim on any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised during that inter partes review.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §315(e)(1) can serve as an estoppel precondition to later PTO proceedings (including ex parte reexamination requests) when the petitioner previously raised or reasonably could have raised the same grounds in an IPR. The Director relied on this provision to vacate filings when a requester’s certification (per 37 C.F.R. §1.510(b)(6)) was erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte reexamination initiation and participation rules (35 U.S.C. §§301–307 and regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person at any time may cite prior art and file a request for ex parte reexamination; the Director normally determines within three months whether a 'substantial new question of patentability' (SNQ) is raised (§303(a)); if none, determination is final and nonappealable (§303(c)); if SNQ is found, reexamination ordered (§304) and thereafter the patent owner, and optionally the requester via a reply, participate; requester’s active participation ends with the reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reexamination is conducted according to initial examination procedures (§305). The statutory and regulatory scheme (including 37 C.F.R. §1.550(g)) limits requester role post-reply; only patent owners have an express route for appeal of adverse decisions in reexamination (§306). Understanding who may act and when is central to assessing reviewability and available remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory certification requirement for reexamination requests (37 C.F.R. §1.510(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A reexamination request must include a certification by the third-party requester that the estoppel provisions (e.g., §315(e)(1)) do not prohibit the requester from filing the ex parte reexamination request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the certification is incorrect because §315(e)(1) applies, the Director may vacate the filing dates and proceedings (citing 37 C.F.R. §1.510(d) and MPEP §2227(b)). The Director can use the certification as a basis for vacatur without deciding §303(a) SNQ issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between initiation (non-initiation) decisions and final/post-initiation decisions for non-reviewability analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-reviewability clauses vary in scope: e.g., §314(d) (IPR institution) has broad nonappealability language, while §303(c) (ex parte reexamination no-SNQ denial) is narrower; issues 'closely tied to application and interpretation of statutes related to the Patent Office's decision to initiate' may be nonreviewable (Thryv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must analyze whether the challenged issue is 'closely tied' to an institution decision or instead concerns post-initiation actions; textual differences between non-reviewability provisions are significant, and precedents (Thryv, Cuozzo, SAS) stress parsing those differences rather than treating all initiation-related decisions uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of precedent and analogies (Syntex, Ethicon, Block, Fausto, Elgin, Pregis, Exela)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior cases guide whether Congress intended to preclude review: Syntex interpreted the statute to limit appeals to patent owners for final reexamination decisions; Block and Fausto support preclusion when a party has an administrative route and the statute's scheme is detailed; Thryv and SAS emphasize textual limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply precedents carefully: Syntex supports that requesters cannot appeal final reexamination outcomes but does not control initiation-stage review; Block/Fausto/Elgin-style inferences require close analogy (parallel statutory roles/exhaustion requirements) and cannot be invoked where statutory text lacks clear preclusion. Courts should distinguish cases where plaintiffs had no statutory role or alternative remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic approach for assessing whether statutory scheme precludes review of a particular PTO decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine express text (any explicit non-appealability), the statutory scheme (who is granted review rights, at what stage, and what remedies are available), and legislative history; if Congress affirmatively provided non-reviewability only for specific determinations, do not infer a broader bar without clear indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether Congress afforded alternative procedures or remedies to the party seeking review (e.g., appeal routes for patent owners, mandamus) and whether those alternatives are adequate; but availability of a different remedy (like mandamus) does not alone imply statutory preclusion of APA review. Avoid inferring preclusion from the mere fact that some decisions are made nonappealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional consequences when APA review is precluded
rubrics_metrics.description: If APA review is precluded by statute, the APA's waiver of sovereign immunity does not apply and federal courts lack jurisdiction to entertain the challenge under the APA (citing 5 U.S.C. §701(a)(1) and sovereign immunity principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of preclusion can convert an otherwise final agency action into one for which the plaintiff cannot obtain relief under the APA; courts should therefore decide preclusion questions carefully before reaching the merits. The court here reversed a district-court dismissal that had found preclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of legislative history in determining preclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative history (e.g., House Judiciary Committee report accompanying 1980 enactment) may inform intent but is insufficient to overcome the presumption of reviewability unless it reflects Congress's specific intent relevant to the modern statutory scheme and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical committee statements addressing the statute as originally enacted may not bear on later-added provisions (like §315(e)(1) added by the AIA). Retention of §303(c) in later reforms (AIA) weakens arguments that Congress intended broader preclusion. Ambiguous legislative history should not 'muddy clear statutory language.'
